title: Santa Monica
name: Santa Monica
metaTitle: Santa Monica in Los Angeles, CA
metaDescription: 1031 exchange coordination for Santa Monica office, Third Street Promenade retail, and rent-controlled multifamily on the Los Angeles coastline.

sections.html: Santa Monica combines some of the strictest rent control in the state with a coastal office cluster and a downtown retail corridor still working through a slower post-pandemic recovery. An exchange buyer here needs to treat each of those three markets as its own underwriting exercise rather than assuming Westside pricing applies evenly across the city, since the gap between the strongest and weakest blocks in Santa Monica can be wider than in most Los Angeles submarkets.

sections.heading: A Rent Control Ordinance Stricter Than Its Neighbors
sections.html:
Santa Monica administers its own rent control program through a locally elected board, and its rules on allowable increases and eviction protections are generally tighter than the citywide ordinance covering much of Los Angeles. A multifamily replacement buyer coming from a less-regulated submarket should not assume increase mechanics transfer over, and should have local counsel confirm exactly which units on a target property are covered before finalizing a rent-roll projection.

Capital improvement pass-throughs work differently under this program as well, with limits on how much of a renovation cost can be recovered from tenants and over what period, which changes the payback math on any planned unit turnover renovation. A buyer underwriting a value-add renovation plan for a Santa Monica apartment building should model that pass-through limit explicitly rather than assuming the full renovation cost recovers on the same schedule it would in a less-regulated city.

sections.heading: The Coastal Office Cluster
sections.html:
Santa Monica's office market includes a concentration of media and technology tenants centered near the airport-adjacent business park area, long associated with companies that helped define the coastal tech label for this stretch of Los Angeles. Office rents here have carried a premium over inland Westside submarkets for years, though a replacement buyer should verify current occupancy against a specific tenant's lease term rather than the district's broader reputation.

Several of these office buildings were originally built as aerospace and manufacturing facilities decades ago before converting to creative and technology office space, and a buyer should confirm what structural or mechanical remnants of that earlier use remain, since older concrete tilt-up shells retrofitted for office use sometimes carry higher HVAC and electrical upgrade costs than a building designed as office space from the start.

sections.heading: Third Street Promenade's Uneven Recovery
sections.html: The Third Street Promenade retail corridor has not recovered evenly since the pandemic, with some blocks near full occupancy and others carrying vacant storefronts that have sat empty for extended stretches. A retail replacement buyer targeting this corridor should walk the specific block in question rather than relying on citywide Santa Monica retail data, since performance varies meaningfully from one intersection to the next.

sections.heading: What a Santa Monica List Draws From
sections.html:
Investors building a Santa Monica identification list typically consider:

  • media and technology office space near the airport business park
  • Third Street Promenade and Montana Avenue retail storefronts
  • rent-controlled multifamily buildings under the city's local ordinance
  • limited light-industrial and flex space near the Santa Monica Airport

sections.heading: Development Review as a Timeline Risk
sections.html:
Santa Monica's entitlement and design review process runs slower than in most neighboring cities, and any replacement property that assumes near-term renovation, expansion, or change of use should build that review timeline into the acquisition schedule rather than treating it as a formality. A qualified intermediary coordinating a Santa Monica closing should confirm early whether any planned improvement work needs city approval before the 180-day exchange period closes out.

Buyers who do not have a specific renovation plan in mind should still confirm a building's existing entitlements are current and unexpired, since a lapsed permit or an outdated certificate of occupancy on an older Santa Monica building can turn a routine closing into a longer municipal review process than the exchange timeline was built to absorb.

faqs.q: How does Santa Monica rent control differ from the citywide Los Angeles ordinance?
faqs.a: Santa Monica runs its own locally administered program with a separate elected board, and its allowable increases and eviction protections are generally tighter than the citywide ordinance covering much of Los Angeles, so a buyer should not assume the two rulesets are interchangeable.

faqs.q: Is Santa Monica office space still commanding a premium over the rest of the Westside?
faqs.a: It has historically, largely due to its media and technology tenant concentration near the airport business park, though a buyer should verify current lease terms on a specific building rather than relying on the submarket's general reputation.

faqs.q: Is Third Street Promenade retail a safe 1031 replacement right now?
faqs.a: It depends heavily on the specific block, since recovery since the pandemic has been uneven, with some stretches near full occupancy and others carrying long-vacant storefronts, so a buyer should walk the block and check adjacent vacancy rather than relying on citywide averages.

faqs.q: How does Santa Monica's development review process affect an exchange timeline?
faqs.a: It runs slower than most neighboring cities, so any replacement property with planned renovation or a change of use should have that review timeline built into the acquisition schedule well before the 180-day exchange period ends, and a buyer should confirm current entitlement status even without a renovation plan.

faqs.q: Is there real industrial inventory in Santa Monica?
faqs.a: Very limited. What exists tends to be light-industrial or flex space near the airport, and investors looking for meaningful industrial product typically look elsewhere in the South Bay or the broader Los Angeles market, where land is less constrained and buildings run larger.
